cells.tense: You are at the bench, and the shape you set is holding.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Pick an arrangement you already keep — a routine, a shelf, a way you run a task — and tend it this week with fresh hands, seeing what it asks for now instead of what you decided when you built it.
cells.core:
You can put a shape down for what comes next and then let it work. The plan goes in, the frame holds, and you don't keep reopening it — you let the structure carry the weight it was built for and you step back from the detail. Fewer decisions, not more.

The sign that it's going well is that a thing set up well doesn't need your hand on it every hour. Take some arrangement you already run — a routine, a corner, a way you've done a task a hundred times — and this week tend it as a learner would, with fresh eyes, seeing what it asks for today. Building and tending are different jobs.

cells.tense: The next structure is going up in your head before this one has held anything.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Take the next thing that lands on you and set out plainly what happened, in sequence, leaving feelings off the page. Read it back before deciding. Let the page show you the shape before you build on it.
cells.core:
You lay the frame before the ground is settled. The pattern goes down fast, one structure rises, and your attention has already moved to reworking the next before the first has held a single thing. The method itself is sound — where you are, it is running well out in front of what it was meant to serve.

A slower, smaller move undoes the running ahead. Next time something lands, put on the page only what is true and what came before what, with none of the feelings included, and read it back. The facts already have a shape. You don't have to bring one with you.

cells.tense: You stood at the threshold of building, and that moment is already behind you.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Find a step you can already see, small and clearly doable, and do it properly. Not a plan around it. Just that single step, laid down well, and then stop there.
cells.core:
Setting a pattern has stalled. The window for putting the shape down closed, and you are still at the door of it, holding what could have been built and going over why it wasn't. What you can do well right now is small and solid, not comprehensive.

Pick a step that's already visible to you — something you know how to do, no framework behind it — and do it properly, once. Not the whole structure. One laid brick. Strength in a life comes back this way, from doing a clear thing well, not from designing the thing you'll do once the timing is better.
cells.sheetLine: The moment passed. One solid step is still yours.

cells.tense: The pattern is being set, and the hand setting it isn't being counted.
cells.act: care for it with fresh hands and see what it needs
cells.ask: Return to an arrangement you've kept running — a routine, a system, a way your days work — and this week examine it as if you'd just arrived. Notice what it needs now, and give it that.
cells.core:
The structures around you hold, and it reads as nobody in particular holding them. What you decide about how things are arranged tends to simply become how things are arranged. The shape is yours, and the account of it has been filed under no one.

Go back to an arrangement you've been keeping running and look at it with fresh hands, as though you had walked in and knew none of the reasons behind it. See what it actually asks for now, and adjust it to that. No account of yourself to correct. Just the structure, tended by the one who set it.
cells.sheetLine: The shape is yours even when it reads as no one's.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person has authority over how things are set up for other people — the seat says pattern-making is the capacity, but the record gives no evidence it is being used on anyone but themselves, so all asks stay on the person's own structures. A reader could reasonably say 'I don't build patterns for other people, I just keep my own life together,' and the cells should survive that because each ask names a thing they might already do for themselves. The ask survives a wrong read because tending, fact-writing, and one solid step are useful whether or not the diagnosis lands, and each can be practised alone without money or a safe person. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about building for others; none appear.
